opus-5.5.text:
I think CUDA deserves enormous credit. Before CUDA, if you wanted to do general-purpose computing on a GPU, you basically had to disguise your computation as a graphics problem: pack your data into textures and write shaders. CUDA changed that. It gave people a C-like programming model with threads, blocks, and shared memory that maps quite directly onto the hardware. That's why it became the foundation for almost everything in deep learning and scientific computing on GPUs today.

But CUDA is fundamentally a low-level tool. To get really good performance you have to think about memory coalescing, occupancy, bank conflicts, synchronization, and you're writing C++ with all its compile-and-debug overhead. That's fine for a small group of experts, but most of the people who need high performance are physicists, graphics researchers, ML engineers, and students. They live in Python. They want to iterate quickly, visualize results, and not spend a week chasing a segfault in a kernel.

So I see CUDA as the assembly language, or maybe the C, of this era of parallel computing. It's the layer everything rests on, but most people shouldn't write it directly most of the time. The trend we're seeing, with things like Taichi, Numba, Triton, JAX, and others, is to put a Python frontend on top and let a compiler handle the hard parts. You write something that looks like ordinary Python, and the system just-in-time compiles it into efficient GPU code, often generating CUDA or PTX underneath.

That was really the motivation behind Taichi. When I was doing physical simulation research, I kept running into the same trade-off: either write fast but painful C++ and CUDA, or write easy but slow Python. I didn't think that trade-off was necessary. If the compiler understands your data structures and your parallel loops, it can do a lot of the optimization a human CUDA expert would do: loop parallelization, memory layout, sparse data structure handling. It can do it automatically, and it can target multiple backends, not just NVIDIA.

Portability is another point. CUDA is tied to one vendor. As we get more diverse hardware, like Apple GPUs, AMD, mobile chips, and various accelerators, a higher-level abstraction lets you write the program once and run it in many places. Python-embedded domain-specific languages are a natural fit for that.

So CUDA isn't going away. It will remain critical for people building the infrastructure and squeezing out the last few percent of performance. But I believe the center of gravity for most developers is moving up the stack, toward Python with smart compilers underneath. CUDA becomes more of a compilation target than something everyone writes by hand. I think that's a healthy evolution. It lets far more people get access to the power of parallel hardware.

r001.rationale: The response describes CUDA as providing a C-like programming model, but does not clearly say that its syntax is close to C or C++ in order to make GPU programming accessible to programmers familiar with those languages.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention PyTorch or characterize how it uses Python syntax for high-performance computing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think CUDA deserves enormous credit. It's the reason GPUs became general-purpose computing devices at all, and almost everything we do in high-performance computing today, including Taichi, sits on top of the ecosystem NVIDIA built around it. So I don't see CUDA as something to be replaced. I see it as the foundation layer.

But CUDA was designed for a certain kind of programmer. It assumes you're comfortable with C++, that you'll think about memory hierarchies, thread blocks, warps, and synchronization yourself. That's a lot of cognitive overhead, and it means the number of people who can actually write good GPU code is very small compared to the number of people who need high performance. When I was doing graphics and physical simulation research, I kept noticing that my colleagues had great ideas but spent most of their time fighting the tooling instead of testing the ideas.

That's really the gap Python-based approaches are trying to close. Python has become the language of science and machine learning, not because it's fast, but because it's productive and the community is enormous. The question is whether you can keep that productivity and still get close to the performance of hand-written CUDA. With Taichi, our bet was that you can, if you let people write imperative, parallel code in Python syntax and then have a compiler do the heavy lifting: generating kernels, handling data layout, running the same code on CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, or just CPUs.

So in the evolution you're describing, I'd frame it like this. CUDA is the assembly language of the GPU era, in a good sense. It's expressive, close to the metal, and it will always be there for people who need every last percent. Python-based systems like Taichi, Triton, JAX and others are the higher-level layer that makes that power accessible to ten or a hundred times more people. Most of them still compile down to CUDA or PTX in the end. What changes is who gets to participate, how fast you can iterate, and how portable your code is.

And honestly, I think the two will keep converging. NVIDIA itself is investing heavily in Python-first interfaces now, which tells you the direction. The long-term picture is probably not CUDA versus Python, but Python as the front door and CUDA, or whatever comes after it, as the engine room.

r001.rationale: The response says CUDA assumes familiarity with C++, but does not explain that its syntax stays close to C or C++ to make GPU programming accessible.

r002.rationale: PyTorch is not mentioned or characterized; the response discusses Taichi, Triton, and JAX instead.

astra-6.text:
I think CUDA is an important foundation for that evolution. It gives you a lot of control over the GPU, but getting good performance requires understanding things like memory access, parallelism, and synchronization. That’s a lot to ask of someone whose main goal is to implement an algorithm.

Python-based high-performance programming can raise that level of abstraction. You express the computation in a more accessible language, and a compiler handles more of the work of mapping it to the hardware. Python itself doesn’t have to execute the performance-critical operations.

So I don’t see this as Python simply replacing CUDA. CUDA remains useful for low-level control and highly tuned kernels. The opportunity is to make GPU performance accessible to more people, while preserving a path to that control when they need it.

r001.rationale: The response says CUDA provides low-level GPU control, but does not explain its accessibility to C or C++ programmers or mention its syntax being close to those languages.

r002.rationale: The response discusses Python-based high-performance programming generally, but does not mention PyTorch or say it repurposes Python syntax extensively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think CUDA has played a very important role. It gave programmers a way to express general-purpose computation on GPUs and get very high performance. But you still need to understand a lot of hardware details, and that creates a pretty high barrier for people who primarily work in Python.

The next step, to me, is to let people describe their computation in a language they’re comfortable with, while the compiler takes on more of that work. Python can be the interface without the computation running in the Python interpreter. You compile the performance-critical parts into efficient GPU code.

So I don’t see it as Python simply replacing CUDA. It’s more an evolution in the level of abstraction. CUDA gives you control; a good Python-based system should make that performance accessible to more people, while still letting you go deeper when you need to.

r001.rationale: The response says CUDA enables general-purpose GPU computation and has a high hardware-learning barrier, but does not explain its C/C++-like syntax or accessibility to C/C++ programmers.

r002.rationale: It discusses Python as an interface for compiled GPU code, but does not mention PyTorch or characterize its extensive use of Python syntax for high-performance computing.
